```{r}
#| label: setup-plot-style
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(showtext)   # install.packages("showtext")

# slide fonts (downloaded from Google Fonts at render time)
font_add_google("Ubuntu", "ubuntu", regular.wt = 300, bold.wt = 500)
font_add_google("Roboto Slab", "robotoslab", regular.wt = 300, bold.wt = 700)
font_add_google("Yanone Kaffeesatz", "yanone", regular.wt = 400, bold.wt = 700)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.showtext = TRUE)

# slide colors (econpol_slides.scss)
pal <- c(blue = "#5d8198", red = "#e76254", dred = "#d03161", yellow = "#ffd500",
         green = "#218500", brown = "#d37b00",
         grey200 = "#e9ecef", grey400 = "#ced4da", grey500 = "#adb5bd",
         grey600 = "#868e96", grey800 = "#343a40", grey900 = "#212529")

# ordered palette from blue to red, for many ordered categories
pal_ramp <- function(n) colorRampPalette(c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["red"]]))(n)

# ggplot theme matching the slides:
# Ubuntu for text, Roboto Slab for numbers, Yanone Kaffeesatz in red for titles
theme_econpol <- function(base_size = 12,
                          text_x = TRUE, text_y = TRUE,      # axis text (tick labels)
                          title_x = TRUE, title_y = TRUE) {  # axis titles
  th <- theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "ubuntu") +
    theme(
      text          = element_text(colour = pal[["grey800"]]),
      panel.grid    = element_blank(),
      axis.text     = element_text(family = "robotoslab", colour = pal[["grey600"]],
                                   size = rel(0.85)),
      axis.title.x  = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
      axis.title.y  = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
      plot.title    = element_text(family = "yanone", colour = pal[["red"]],
                                   size = rel(1.8), margin = margin(b = 6)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = pal[["grey600"]]),
      plot.caption  = element_text(family = "robotoslab", colour = pal[["grey600"]],
                                   size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title    = element_blank(),
      legend.key.width = unit(1, "null")
    )
  if (!text_x)  th <- th + theme(axis.text.x  = element_blank())
  if (!text_y)  th <- th + theme(axis.text.y  = element_blank())
  if (!title_x) th <- th + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank())
  if (!title_y) th <- th + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())
  th
}
```

# Central Banks

## What do central banks do? 


:::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.column .hl .hl-blue style="width: 33%; padding: 0.5em 1em; isolation: isolate;"}
- Interest rates

- Payments systems

- [Lending]{.marker-hl} to private banks

- Regulation and oversight
:::

::: {.column .hl .hl-dred style="width: 33%; padding: 0.5em 1em; isolation: isolate;"}
- Inflation

- Growth and employment

- Financial markets and institutions

- Interest and exchange rates
:::

::: {.column .hl .hl-green style="width: 33%; padding: 0.5em 1em; isolation: isolate;"}
- Independent

- Accountable

- Transparent
:::

::::

## Historical concepts

Central banks go back to the 17th century. Some rulers relied on them for financing, others to regulate the financial system. Until the mid-20th century, most countries did not have a central bank. Almost all had mints that monopolized money production though.

- **Government bank**: Issues currency.

- **Monetary policy**: Influence interest rates.

- **Bankers' bank**: Holds deposits of private banks.

## Bankers' bank

The central bank hardly interacts with individual customers. It mostly takes deposits, extends credit and auctions off bonds to financial institutions.

- **Lender of last resort**: Lends money to keep credit market going.

- **Manages payments system**: With bank notes ensure that they are circulated, with economic payments ensure they clear.

- **Oversees commercial banks**: Regulate institutions, inspect banks, stress-test system.

## What the ECB cannot do

The ECB is tasked with [monetary policy]{.marker-hl}, but not fiscal policy. 

It cannot determine, and should not influence, [budgets or economic policy]{.marker-hl}.

It does not collect taxes or generate income beyond [seignorage]{.marker-hl}

## Stability

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
Financial markets tend to: 

- Episodes of high volatility.

- Vicious cycles of increased risk-taking.

- Financial instability.

- International imbalances.
:::
:::{.column width=50%}

"*The central bank is essentially part of the government.*" (Cecchetti and Schönholtz 2021)

Central banks are tasked with stabilizing the system, expressed in interest rates, price levels, exchange rates, even employment and economic growth.
:::
::::

## Inflation

Traditionally, price stability has been the primary objective of central banks (e.g. ECB). They are supposed to curb price effects of fiscal expansion, import price, profit or wage pressure.

- **Interest rates**: Central banks make lending more expensive, curbing capital accumulation and wage growth, decreasing demand.

- **Lending**: Credit freezes lead to deflation, central banks step in to re-start the lending cycle.

## Central bank independence

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[{{< fa plus >}}]{.hl .hl-green .secfont style="font-size:1.3rem;"}

- No short term policy goals that outweigh long term development.

- No electoral pressure to increase fiscal spending with danger of demand outrunning supply.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
[{{< fa minus >}}]{.hl .hl-dred .secfont style="font-size:1.3rem;"}

- No democratic oversight or democratic legitimacy.

- Recruits from finance or academia with ingrained class interest.
:::
::::

## European Central Bank {.smaller}

## European Central Bank

The **European Central Bank** oversees a system of national central banks through anonymous votes of the [governing council]{.marker-hl}. Its role and independence is largely codified in the [Maastricht accords]{.marker-hl}. Its **primary objective** is [price stability]{.marker-hl}. Secondary objectives include supporting growth and employment as long as it does not run counter to price stability.

- **Owned** by the NCBs.

- Carries out **monetary policy** (relationships with commercial banks) through the NCBs.

- **Sells and purchases securities** but also supplies [collateralized lending]{.marker-hl} to banks.

## The Austrian National Bank

**OeNB** was [founded in 1923]{.marker-hl}, operating as Austria's central bank and allocating foreign economic assistance to Austria.

It is an [Aktiengesellschaft]{.marker-hl}, with all shares owned by the **Republic of Austria** since 2010. Before 2010 it was co-owned by the Republic, Wirtschaftskammer and Arbeiterkammer.

The OeNB and **Financial Markets Authority (FMA)** participate in the European Central Bank as well as the European Systemic Risk Board.

## Division of labor {.smaller}

::::{.columns}
:::{.column}
**ECB**

- Target **interest rates**

- Central **analysis**

- Since 2014: **single supervisory mechanism** for [larger banks]{.marker-hl}
:::
:::{.column}
**NCBs**

- **Operate** monetary policy

- Issue and administer **banknotes**

- National communication

- Supervise smaller banks and non-Eurosystem tasks.
:::
::::

## Central banks' balance sheets {.smaller}

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**Assets**

- **Securities**, mostly treasury issued, since 2007 increasingly risk assets.

- **Foreign currency reserves** to stabilize exchange rates.

- **Loans** to commerical banks.
:::
:::{.column width=50%}
**Liabilities**

- **Currency**: all issued [bank notes]{.marker-hl} are redeemable.

- **Government account**: The government's bank account.

- Commercial bank **deposits** and reserves.
:::
::::

## Central bank transactions {.smaller}

- **Open market operations**: Buy/sell [securities]{.marker-hl}

- **Foreign exchange intervention**: Buy/sell currency reserves.

- **Extend loans** to commercial banks.

- **Pay out cash** to account holders (government or banks).

## Unconventional monetary policy {.smaller}

When the [global financial crisis of 2007-2009]{.marker-hl} unfurled, both the Fed and the ECB introduced new central bank instruments dubbed **unconventional monetary policy**. They are usually legitimized by conventional interest rates approaching the [zero lower bound]{.marker-hl}.

This included **targeted asset purchases** (e.g. of mortgage backed securities) rather than broad interventions; **targeted long-term refinancing operations** as cheap credit to warm up credit freezes; and most famously, **quantitative easing**

## Quantitative easing {.smaller}

Quantitative easing **supplies reserves** to commercial banks beyond the assumed supply/demand relationship that sets the target rate.

The goal of quantitative easing is to supply firms and consumers with money through bank operations.

## Quantitative easing {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: fig-qe
#| fig-cap: "Schematic illustration of post-2007 quantitative easing in the United States"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

# --- geometry -------------------------------------------------------------
ioer    <- 1                          # IOER rate (floor)
x_start <- 0.3; y_start <- 9.5        # top-left start of reserve demand
x_B     <- 6                          # demand becomes flat at B
x_07    <- 3                          # reserve supply 2007
x_15    <- 7.6                        # reserve supply 2015 (point C)
slope   <- (ioer - y_start) / (x_B - x_start)
target  <- y_start + slope * (x_07 - x_start)   # 2007 target rate (point A)

col_d <- pal[["red"]]    # demand
col_s <- pal[["blue"]]   # supply
txt   <- 4.2         # text size
fam   <- "ubuntu"

ggplot() +
  # axes
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0, y = 0, yend = 10.6,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 8.6, y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
  # dashed guide lines
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = x_07, y = target, yend = target,
           linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[["grey500"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = x_B, y = ioer, yend = ioer,
           linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[["grey500"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  # reserve supply (vertical)
  annotate("segment", x = c(x_07, x_15), xend = c(x_07, x_15),
           y = 0, yend = 9.9, colour = col_s, linewidth = 0.9) +
  # reserve demand (kinked)
  annotate("path", x = c(x_start, x_B, 8.6), y = c(y_start, ioer, ioer),
           colour = col_d, linewidth = 0.9) +
  # points A and C
  annotate("point", x = c(x_07, x_15), y = c(target, ioer),
           colour = col_d, size = 2) +
  # shift arrow
  annotate("segment", x = 3.6, xend = 7.0, y = 9.1, yend = 9.1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  # supply labels with subscripts
  annotate("text", x = x_07, y = 10.4, label = "Reserve~Supply[2007]",
           parse = TRUE, family = fam, size = txt) +
  annotate("text", x = x_15, y = 10.4, label = "Reserve~Supply[2015]",
           parse = TRUE, family = fam, size = txt) +
  # point labels
  annotate("text", x = x_07 + 0.2, y = target + 0.3, label = "A",
           hjust = 0, family = fam, size = txt) +
  annotate("text", x = c(x_B, x_15), y = -0.4, label = c("B", "C"),
           family = fam, size = txt) +
  # scale of QE
  annotate("segment", x = x_B + 0.25, xend = x_15 - 0.25, y = -0.4, yend = -0.4,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), ends = "both", type = "open"),
           linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = (x_B + x_15) / 2, y = -1.1, label = "Scale of QE",
           family = fam, size = txt) +
  # demand label
  annotate("text", x = 5.6, y = 3.6, label = "Reserve\nDemand",
           hjust = 0.3, lineheight = 1.1, family = fam, size = txt) +
  # axis labels
  annotate("text", x = -0.15, y = c(target, ioer),
           label = c("2007 Target Rate", "IOER Rate"),
           hjust = 1, family = fam, size = txt) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.15, y = 10.3, label = "Market Federal\nFunds Rate",
           hjust = 1, lineheight = 0.95, family = fam, size = txt) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.7, y = -0.6, label = "Quantity of Reserves",
           family = fam, size = txt) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8.6), ylim = c(-1.3, 10.8),
                  expand = FALSE, clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 10, 110),
        text = element_text(colour = pal[["grey800"]]))
```

# Geometries

## Grammar of graphics {.smaller}

In this course, we mainly work with the [ggplot2]{.marker-hl} R package. The **gg** stands for **Wilkinson's grammar of graphic**. For now it will suffice to understand the basic categories of this grammar.

- **Variables** secribe the underlying data structure.

- **Algebra** are operations that combine variables.

- **Geometry** create [graphical shapes]{.marker-hl} from variables.

- **Aesthetics** assign data to dimensions of the data - e.g. [x- and y-axis]{.marker-hl}, color, or size.

- **Statistics** are [functions]{.marker-hl} that change the appearance of geometries.

- **Scales** represent variables in different dimensions (e.g. the stretching of axis or color palettes).

- **Coordinates** are a mapping of graphs onto the 2 dimensional representation we perceive as plots.

## Geometries {.smaller}

**Geometries** (in ggplot2: [geoms]{.marker-hl}) are an intuitive concept: The shapes we choose to visualize.

```{r}
#| label: data-geoms
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(42)
countries <- c("AT","BE","DE","ES","FR","IT","NL","PT","GR","SK","EE","HR")
dates <- seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2025-12-01"), by = "month")

# common policy path (stylized): flat, hike, plateau, cut, flat
knots <- as.Date(c("2015-01-01", "2022-07-01", "2023-09-01",
                   "2024-06-01", "2025-06-01", "2025-12-01"))
dfr <- approx(x = as.numeric(knots),
              y = c(-0.5, -0.5, 4, 4, 2, 2),
              xout = as.numeric(dates))$y
policy <- tibble(date = dates, dfr = dfr)

# common inflation shock peaking late 2022
infl_common <- 1.2 + 8 * exp(-((as.numeric(dates - as.Date("2022-10-01")) / 240)^2))

panel <- expand_grid(country = countries, date = dates) |>
  left_join(policy, by = "date") |>
  group_by(country) |>
  mutate(
    shock_sens    = runif(1, 0.6, 1.8),     # countries differ in exposure
    passthrough   = runif(1, 0.5, 0.9),     # and in rate pass-through
    inflation     = infl_common[match(date, dates)] * shock_sens + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.4),
    mortgage_rate = 1.5 + passthrough * (dfr + 0.5) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.15),
    unemployment  = runif(1, 4, 12) - 0.15 * inflation + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.3)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    date < as.Date("2022-01-01") ~ "Negative rates",
    date < as.Date("2024-01-01") ~ "Tightening",
    TRUE ~ "Easing"
  ) |> factor(levels = c("Negative rates", "Tightening", "Easing"))) |>
  select(date, country, period, dfr, inflation, mortgage_rate, unemployment)
```

## geom_bar

```{r}
#| label: plot-geombar
#| fig-cap: "Bar Charts for comparing mean inflation rates between countries."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

panel |> 
  group_by(country) |> 
  summarize(inflation=mean(inflation, na.rm=TRUE)) |> 
  mutate(country=fct_reorder(country, inflation)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_col(aes(y=country, x=inflation, 
               fill=(country=="AT"))) +
  geom_text(aes(y=country, 
                x=inflation + .5, 
                label=sprintf("%.2f%%", inflation)),
            family="robotoslab",
            color=pal[["grey800"]],
            size=3.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=mean(panel$inflation, na.rm=TRUE), 
             linetype=3, 
             color=pal[["grey600"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("FALSE"=pal[["blue"]], "TRUE"=pal[["dred"]]),
                    guide="none") +
  theme_econpol(text_x=FALSE, text_y=FALSE, title_x=FALSE, title_y=FALSE)
```

## geom_bar

```{r ref.label="plot-geombar", echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
```

## geom_line

```{r}
#| label: plot-geomline
#| fig-cap: "Line Plot to illustrate the development of inflation and the deposit facility rate in Austria."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

panel |> 
  filter(country=="AT") |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(x=date, y=dfr), color=pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(x=date, y=inflation), color=pal[["red"]], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text",
           x=as.Date("2020-01-01"), 
           y=3, 
           label="Inflation", 
           color=pal[["red"]],
           family="ubuntu") +
  annotate("text", 
           x=as.Date("2024-10-01"), 
           y=1, 
           label="Deposit Facility Rate", 
           color=pal[["blue"]],
           family="ubuntu") +
  annotate("text", 
           y=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(inflation==max(inflation)) |> 
                pull(inflation) |> 
                max()) 
           + .5,
           x=(panel |>
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(inflation==max(inflation)) |>
                pull(date) |> 
                min()),
           label=sprintf("%.1f%%", panel |> 
                           filter(country=="AT") |> 
                           filter(inflation==max(inflation)) |> 
                           pull(inflation) |> 
                           max()),
           color=pal[["red"]],
           family="robotoslab"
  ) +
    annotate("text", 
           y=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(date==min(date)) |> 
                pull(inflation) |> 
                max()) 
           + 1.5,
           x=(panel |>
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(date==min(date)) |>
                pull(date) |> 
                min()),
           label=sprintf("%.1f%%", panel |> 
                           filter(country=="AT") |> 
                           filter(date==min(date)) |> 
                           pull(inflation) |> 
                           max()),
           color=pal[["red"]],
           family="robotoslab"
  ) +
  annotate("text", 
           y=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(dfr==max(dfr)) |> 
                pull(dfr) |> 
                max()) + .5,
           x=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(dfr==max(dfr)) |> 
                pull(date) |> 
                max()),
           label=sprintf("%.1f%%", 
                         panel |> 
                           filter(country=="AT") |> 
                           filter(dfr==max(dfr)) |> 
                           pull(dfr) |> 
                           max()),
           color=pal[["blue"]],
           family="robotoslab"
  ) +
    annotate("text", 
           y=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(date==min(date)) |> 
                pull(dfr) |> 
                max()) + .5,
           x=(panel |> 
                filter(country=="AT") |> 
                filter(date==min(date)) |> 
                pull(date) |> 
                max()),
           label=sprintf("%.1f%%", 
                         panel |> 
                           filter(country=="AT") |> 
                           filter(date==min(date)) |> 
                           pull(dfr) |> 
                           max()),
           color=pal[["blue"]],
           family="robotoslab"
  ) +
  theme_econpol(text_y=FALSE, title_x=FALSE, title_y=FALSE) +
  theme(axis.line.x=element_line(color=pal[["grey500"]]))
```

## geom_point

```{r}
#| label: plot-geompoint
#| fig-cap: "Scatter Plot to illustrate the relationship of deposit facility rates and mortgage rates."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

panel |> 
  mutate(country=fct_reorder(country, mortgage_rate, .fun=mean, na.rm=TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x=dfr, y=mortgage_rate, color=country), 
             alpha=0.3, 
             size=4) +
  scale_color_manual(values=pal_ramp(n_distinct(panel$country))) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2,
         override.aes = list(alpha = 1)
          )
         ) +
  labs(x="Deposit Facility Rate", y="Mortgage Rate") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(1,3,5)) +
  theme_econpol()
```

## geom_density

```{r}
#| label: plot-geomdensity
#| fig-cap: "Density Plot to illustrate the differences of country inflation rates under the same regime."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

panel |> 
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x=inflation, fill=period), alpha=0.6, color=NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Negative rates"=pal[["blue"]],
                             "Tightening"=pal[["red"]],
                             "Easing"=pal[["grey500"]])) +
  labs(x="Inflation") +
  theme_econpol(text_y=FALSE, title_y=FALSE)
```
